newsitem.title: USA: Champion Q1 shortfall seen as non-recurring.
newsitem.headline: Champion Q1 shortfall seen as non-recurring.

text.p: Champion Enterprises Inc, which saw its shares drop after it estimated lower than expected first-quarter earnings, is not slumping because of problems with its business fundamentals, analysts said Monday.

"I'm convinced this (stock decline) is a one-time event," Jasmine Perry, an analyst at Goldman Sachs, said. "Investors seem to be looking for weakness in the industry, but the demand for this type of lower-end housing is fine."
Earlier, Champion said its earnings in the first quarter will be about $0.28 a share, less than the consensus of $0.32.

Champion, which makes manufactured homes and medium-duty buses, cited reduced sales and income after a restructuring of its home product line, in addition to startup expenses at three plants, for the earnings shortfall.
Goldman's Perry said the startup costs, estimated by Champion at $0.04 a share, were larger than the company expected.
Perry added that the company's new home products in the wake of the realignment were not well received by dealers, causing a revamping of the line and higher costs.
"This company's fundamentals are so sound, I don't believe the activity we're seeing today is warranted," Perry said.
David Lee Smith, an analyst at Hoak Breedlove Wesneski, agreed the sell-off was an overreaction by the market.
"The magnitude of the decline makes no sense to us," he said. "This is one of the most solid companies in the manufactured homes (sector) with a squeaky clean balance sheet."
Dean Gulis, an analyst at Roney & Co, agreed the Champion decline is a one-time event, but he cautioned that a drop in manufactured housing sales remains a threat to investors.
"The risk (for investors) will not be what's going on internally at Champion Enterprises," he said. "The bigger issue is how strong the overall market for manufactured housing will be."
Gulis said he believes manufactured home companies cannot sustain the double-digit growth seen in the last few years. He predicted growth will be in the single digits in 1997.
Perry, the Goldman Sachs analyst, agreeed.
"I see demand growing by five to seven percent," she said. "(The industry) seems to be unaffected by recent interest rate increases that pushed rates up to about 14 percent.
Champion shares were off 3-1/2 Monday afternoon at 14-5/8. Company officials were not available to comment on the stock activity.
